title: Is Amazon's Profit Riskier Than It Looks?

Is Amazon's Profit Riskier Than It Looks?

Today's big story: Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92?

Update, Nov 23: Large tech stocks rose in Monday morning trading after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Amazon rose about 4%, to about $256, and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) rose about 7%, while Anthropic was about flat. The figures below are at Friday's close.

Amazon.com (AMZN) closed at $246.82 on Friday, Nov 20. That was a fall of 4.1% for the day. Anthropic (ANT), newly listed, fell 8.5% on its second day of trading. Why mention both? This article looks at how much of Amazon's profit came from gains on stocks and stakes it holds, and what a slide like Anthropic's could mean for that profit.

The answer is a large share. Over the four quarters to September 2026, 40.1% of Amazon's pre-tax income was non-operating income. That is profit from outside the business itself, such as gains on stocks and stakes a company owns. Almost all of it was gains on securities, $69.7 billion.

That is new for Amazon. From 2019 to 2022, non-operating items were a small net loss, -6.0% of pre-tax income. From 2023 to September 2025, they were 9.3% of pre-tax income. So Amazon's reported profit now rises and falls with the prices of what it holds. The income statements do not show which holdings produced the gains. So we do not size any single one, Anthropic included.

Which Quarter Brought In Most Of The Gains?

Most of it came in one quarter. In the three months to June 2026, Amazon's non-operating income was $53.4 billion. That was 66.0% of its pre-tax income. It was also the largest of any quarter since the start of 2019.

Net income that quarter was $62.6 billion. Operating income, the profit from selling goods and services, was $27.5 billion. So net income was 2.3 times operating income.

Amazon's net income in the three months to June was 2.3 times its operating income. If Amazon is a big part of your savings, the profit it reports can drop fast when the stocks it holds fall. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.

Net income also ran 1.4 times operating cash flow that quarter. Operating cash flow is the cash the business brings in from customers after its running costs.

Did The Gains Keep Coming After June?

No. In the three months to September, Amazon had a non-operating loss of $1.2 billion. Gains on securities became a loss of $0.7 billion. Operating income that quarter was $28.1 billion.

For a while this morning, Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) looked like it would soar today after news of Jensen Huang's dramatic return to Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) broke. Shares of the newly public company opened up 5.4%.

But by the closing bell, Anthropic was down 1.4%. Not a bad day per se, but consider the gains from the rest of the tech market:

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia: up 31.5%

Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU): up 19%

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META): up 6.6%

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL): up 6%

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN): up 3.5%

Just two trading days after its debut, in what was the year's biggest gain for the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC), Anthropic stock inched lower. Why did the Claude maker's stock miss out on most of the marketwide rally?

Why Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia lifted the stock market

Nvidia's board announced this morning that it was bringing Huang back as CEO, president, and board member. That's just under a week after Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that Huang's return was not on the table. The official announcement said that the board had "received input from senior levels of the United States government," giving it confidence that "Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

The government input was, in fact, from the most senior of senior levels: the U.S. President. Trump told CNBC that he spoke with the board "directly and indirectly" to advocate for Huang's return: "I convinced them." Trump reassured the board that he did not pose a national security threat after Attorney General Todd Blanche assured the President that investigators had no evidence to suggest wrongdoing.

Whatever the full reasoning behind that led to the board's decision, the move -- a shock to many -- breathed life into an ailing AI trade that was in serious need of good news; the Nasdaq turned red for 2026 on Friday after entering a correction earlier in the month.

Why open-weight AI models could threaten Anthropic stock

So why did Anthropic sit this one out?

A few reasons: first, Reuters reported that President Trump -- Vice President JD Vance, too -- intervened in part because they saw Huang as crucial to keeping American companies competitive in open-weight AI -- a market in which China leads.

Open-weight models are offered to the public -- often for free -- to download, tweak, adapt, and run however and wherever they see fit.

Nvidia's board, which until last week maintained it would not reinstate Huang to his prior position, reversed its decision and reappointed Jensen Huang as CEO with immediate effect. "I can't wait to get back to work," Huang said.

The dramatic return follows less than a fortnight after Huang stepped down over an admitted relationship with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, which led to a tumultuous stretch during which the semiconductor giant's shares recorded their worst weekly performance since 2008.

Following the announcement, Trump, in a Truth Social post, welcomed the Nvidia board's decision.

"The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Trump wrote, adding that the country needs Huang's leadership to support Nvidia and the broader American economy.

"The reinstatement of the prolific leader of Nvidia's AI buildout as CEO is bolstering confidence that the momentum of modern technology will remain robust, while sidelining fears of a slowdown," Jose Torres at Interactive Brokers told Bloomberg.

Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, used the November 20 episode of his podcast, The Real Eisman Playbook, to argue that the AI market has changed: "Without Nvidia backstopping the AI stack, AI is no longer one trade. And that's why stock picking is back, and valuation is back."

Shutterstock

Three days later, the board of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and the stock rose 32.36% in today's session. Does his return undo Eisman's thesis? The price data suggests the split he described had already happened.

NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Why Eisman Says NVIDIA Held the AI Trade Together

Eisman's argument centers on circular financing. He said Huang took equity stakes in, or lent money to, companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, CoreWeave and Nebius Group, and those companies then used the money to buy NVIDIA chips. "He created, I think, a virtual vertical holding company," Eisman said. When one balance sheet supports the whole network, having any AI stock means having a piece of the same machine. Once that support passes, Eisman said, the companies "need to be evaluated on their own merits and not as part of a larger whole."

Today's big story: Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92?

Snap (SNAP) stock lost 28.3% from October 22 to November 20, 2026, while the S&P 500 fell 9.7%. The steepest drop came on November 5, when the shares fell 14.0% the day after Snap's third-quarter report missed on revenue and daily active users. So when markets have fallen before, how much harder was Snap hit, and how long did it stay down?

Snap Has Fallen Deeper Than The Market Each Time

Snap has traded through eight market shocks since it listed in 2017. Its average fall in them was 43.4%, against 15.3% for the S&P 500. Snap was hit hardest in the 2022 inflation shock, falling 83% while the index fell 24%. That fall included two days, May 24 and July 22, 2022, when the stock closed 35% or more below the day before. In the 2020 COVID-19 crash, Snap fell 51% against 34% for the index.

Snap's 83% fall in 2022 wiped out most of what its holders had. If a big share of your savings sits in Snap, a drop like that is hard to sit through. In a free 30-minute review, our partner advisory firm can show you ways to limit your loss if the stock falls further and to sell with a smaller tax bill. Book the free review.

Snap got back to its peak close in five of those eight shocks, a median of 1.9 months after the low. The slowest of the five, after the 2016-2017 bond selloff, took 39.7 months. That fall came in Snap's first months as a listed company, while the S&P 500 barely moved. The other three falls have not been made back. Measured from the close on the day each of those falls began, Snap's latest close is 90.2% below its close of January 3, 2022. That was not Snap's record close, which came earlier, in September 2021. The latest close is also 73.0% below its close of July 10, 2024, and 57.8% below its close of February 19, 2025.

Losses Have Narrowed As Snap's Revenue Grew

Snap is growing, and it is close to breaking even. Over the four quarters to September 30, 2026, its revenue was $6.57 billion, up 13.8% from a year earlier. Its operating loss narrowed to 1.8% of revenue, from 10.5% a year before. In the third quarter alone, Snap made an operating profit of $76.7 million. Its free cash flow reached $777 million over the twelve months, up from $414 million.

Snap also carries more debt than cash. It held $4.13 billion of debt at the end of September, against $2.77 billion of cash and short-term investments. That debt equals 53.6% of Snap's market value, against 20.3% for the S&P 500.
